passage: With one month left before an audit and no budget for extra hands, Nilesh proposed a small trial: use the AI tools only for documentation and first drafts of unit tests. Nikita, who had doubts about anything near the main code, agreed because of that limit. Each Friday they wrote down two numbers: minutes saved on a task and mistakes found in review. By week two the documentation drafts saved about a third of the time, though Nikita found a test that checked nothing. By week four the pattern was clear: good for docs, useful but needing care for tests. They put it on one page. Nilesh said the critical payment code would stay off limits until a longer trial, and Nikita, still cautious, nodded.

qa.q: Which two numbers did they write down each Friday?
qa.a: They wrote down minutes saved on a task and mistakes found in review.

qa.q: Why did Nikita agree to the trial?
qa.a: Nikita agreed because the limit kept the tools away from the main code, where Nikita had doubts, so Nikita was cautious but willing.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do to ease Nikita's doubts about the test drafts?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask Nikita to review the test drafts and log every weak one, since counting the flaws turns a worry into something measurable.

qa.q: How might a teammate who works on the payment code see the decision?
qa.a: A teammate would probably feel reassured, since the tools stay away from the payment code until a longer trial.

grounding: Shows a team trying AI tools on documentation and unit test drafts for a month, measuring time saved and mistakes, before considering critical code.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: piloting on low-risk tasks first [Action]
passage:
In the Pune office, Sangeeta's team didn't let the AI tools anywhere near the billing code at first. 'One month,' she said at the Monday stand-up. 'Only documentation and first drafts of unit tests. We measure everything.'
Chandrika kept the spreadsheet. For each task: time with the tool, time the usual way, and errors found in review. By the end of the month there were ninety-two entries. Documentation was forty percent faster, with two small errors, both caught. Unit test drafts were thirty percent faster, but reviewers had rejected one in six for testing the wrong thing.
On the last Friday, Sangeeta put the numbers on the screen. 'Docs, yes, we keep going. Tests, yes, with review. Billing code, not yet. We'll pilot that separately, slowly, with more checks.'

qa.q: How many entries were in the spreadsheet by the end of the month?
Why did Sangeeta keep the tools away from billing code, and how did she feel about it?
qa.a: She felt cautious, worried that mistakes in billing code would be costly, so she wanted proof on low-risk work first.

qa.q: What would a sensible next pilot look like?
qa.a: A small, closely reviewed trial on a less critical part of billing, measured the same way before any wider use.

qa.q: How might the reviewers see the pilot?
qa.a: Reviewers caught the weak test drafts, so they may feel their role matters more, not less, with the tools.

grounding: It shows a team trying AI tools on documentation and unit test drafts for a month, measuring time saved and errors before considering critical code.

'Just let everyone use it everywhere,' Gargi said. 'It's faster.'
'Faster at what?' Chandrika asked. 'Show me.'
'I don't have numbers. It feels faster.'
'Then let's get numbers. One month. Low-risk only: writing release notes, drafting unit tests. Nothing in payments or security.'
'And then?'
'You track three things for every task: time with the tool, time without, and anything the reviewer had to fix.'
Four weeks later Gargi walked into Chandrika's cabin with a printout. 'Release notes, half the time, almost no fixes. Unit tests, a third faster, but one in five tested the wrong thing.'
'So?'
'So release notes, yes. Tests, yes, if someone checks them. Payments...' Gargi smiled. 'Not yet.'
Chandrika nodded. 'That's a decision I can defend.'

qa.q: What did Gargi find about unit tests?
qa.a: They were a third faster, but one in five tested the wrong thing.

qa.q: How does Gargi seem to feel by the end?
qa.a: Gargi seems satisfied and a little amused, having turned an excited hunch into a careful, defensible answer.

qa.q: What could the team pilot next, and how?
qa.a: They could try a narrow, well-reviewed use in a less critical service, tracking the same three numbers before touching payments.

qa.q: How does the pilot look to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika gets evidence instead of feelings, which gives a decision that can be defended to others.

grounding: It shows a team piloting AI tools on low-risk tasks for a month and measuring time saved and error rates before wider use in critical code.
